chapter_theme: The killing: lodged with the herdswoman Maadari, Kannaki cooks Kovalan's last meal, he confesses his heedlessness and she her silent endurance, and he goes to sell one anklet; the goldsmith who stole the queen's anklet accuses him, the king orders the thief killed without inquiry, the goldsmith talks down the guards' doubts with a lore of thieves' arts, and a drunken guard cuts Kovalan down; the narrator and the closing venba give the king's bent sceptre and Kovalan's former deed as causes of the one death.

cast.role: Kovalan's wife, lodged with the herdswoman Maadari in Madurai
merchant of Puhar, Kannaki's husband, killed in Madurai
the old herdswoman of Madurai to whom the ascetic Kavunthi entrusted Kannaki (named here as இடைக்குல மடந்தை and தவ்வை)
the herdswomen of Maadari's settlement, acting together
the royal goldsmith of Madurai who accused Kovalan of theft
the Pandya king of Madurai who had Kovalan killed (named here as தென்னவன், வேம்பன், காவலன், மன்னவன்)
the Pandya's guards who carry out the killing
a young spearman among the guards who tells of a thief who took his sword
the drunken, unlettered guard whose sword kills Kovalan

silappathikaram:16:1-16.reading: Glad to have received Kannaki as a ward, the herdswoman Maadari lodges her in a guarded little house apart from the herders' dwellings, has the herdswomen bathe her, tells her that her daughter Aiyai will be her servant and that she will keep her as if wrapped in gold, and so settles her in a place she thinks free of harm.
silappathikaram:16:1-16.nuance: Maadari's praise turns Kannaki's lack of ornament into a beauty that spoils the worth of the Madurai women's gold (செய்யாக் கோலம்), and she bows to her ward. The last line's ஏதம் இல்லா இடம் repeats the word with which Kavunthi judged it safe to leave Kannaki with Maadari (15:124, ஏதம் இன்று), so the 'harmless place' is named on the day of the killing.
silappathikaram:16:1-16.event: Maadari lodges Kannaki in a guarded house, has her bathed and gives her Aiyai as a servant.

silappathikaram:16:17-32.reading: Maadari bids the herdswomen bring at once good vessels for cooking the day's meal, since Kovalan is a lord who keeps the lay disciple's vow, and they bring the vessels with gourds, vegetables, pomegranate, mango and plantain, rice and milk, which Kannaki takes and begins to cut and cook until her face sweats and her eyes redden in the smoky kitchen.
silappathikaram:16:17-32.nuance: சாவக நோன்பிகள் names Kovalan as one under the vow of a lay disciple; in the preceding kaathai the word சாவகர் is used for the lay hearers of the Jain charanas (15:190, 195), and the meal of the day (நாள்வழிப் படூஉம் அடிசில்) may point to the lay rule of eating before dark, though the Tamil does not say so. The merchant's daughter cooking with her own hands, her soft fingers reddening, is the first housekeeping she has done since Puhar. நும்மகனார் and நாத்தூண் நங்கை (the husband's sister) give the herders kin-terms for their guests, but whom each names is not clear.
silappathikaram:16:17-32.event: The herdswomen bring vessels and provisions at Maadari's word, and Kannaki starts cooking.

silappathikaram:16:33-47.reading: With Aiyai lighting the fire, Kannaki cooks with her untrained hands, seats Kovalan on a mat of palm leaf, washes his feet from an earthen bowl, sprinkles water on the ground as if to clear the earth goddess's distress, spreads a young plantain leaf and bids him eat, and he eats after completing the rites proper to the merchant order, while the herders' women begin to wonder whether he is the dark god Yasoda bore.
silappathikaram:16:33-47.nuance: Kovalan, just called a lay disciple under vow, first performs what the sacred text (அருமறை) prescribes for those after kings (அரசர் பின்னோர், the merchant order), so the meal joins a vow-keeper's diet to caste rite without comment. The water sprinkled 'as if to clear the bewilderment of the earth-woman' (மண்ணக மடந்தையை மயக்கொழிப் பனள்போல், line 40) returns at line 215, when the same earth-woman's grief grows under his blood. The unit ends in the middle of the women's question, which runs on into the next.
silappathikaram:16:33-47.event: Kannaki cooks with Aiyai's help, washes Kovalan's feet and serves him, and he eats after his rites.

silappathikaram:16:48-61.reading: Aiyai and her mother marvel that the man eating is the god of the flower-dark hue and the woman the lamp of their own clan who once relieved his distress in the Yamuna, a sight their eyes cannot hold; Kannaki gives Kovalan betel, and he draws her close, asks how her soft feet bore the stony desert path, and wonders aloud what has befallen his old parents and whether this is illusion or a strong former deed.
silappathikaram:16:48-61.nuance: The herders see their guests as Krishna and his herd-clan consort (the Tamil does not name Pinnai here), the pair whose kuravai Maadari will dance in the next kaathai to ward off coming harm. Kovalan's மாயங் கொல்லோ வல்வினை கொல்லோ is a question, not a claim: he does not yet know whether to blame illusion or karma, and in the next lines he blames himself.
silappathikaram:16:48-61.event: Aiyai and Maadari liken the couple to Krishna and his consort; Kovalan, given betel, asks Kannaki how she bore the road.

silappathikaram:16:62-73.reading: Kovalan says his mind is confused and he knows nothing, that keeping company with men of empty talk and idle rakes he grew heedless, that he failed the bidding of his parents and wronged his wise young wife, and asks what she has done in rising to come with him to this city; Kannaki begins her answer, that she had lost the giving to the virtuous, the tending of Brahmins, the receiving of ascetics and the welcoming of guests.
silappathikaram:16:62-73.nuance: Karma and his own fault stand side by side: the line before asked whether this was வல்வினை, and now he names பொச்சாப்பு, bad company and disobedience as his own failures. Lines 65-66 (பொருளுரை யாளர் நச்சுக்கொன் றேற்கும் நன்னெறி யுண்டோ) are hard; they seem to ask whether there is any good way left for one who has spurned the counsel of the wise, but the sense of நச்சு is doubtful. Kannaki's four lost duties are the householder's duties, which she could not keep without her husband.
silappathikaram:16:62-73.event: Kovalan confesses his heedlessness and wrongs, and Kannaki begins to answer.

claims.claim: a wife left by her husband loses the householder's duties of giving to the virtuous, tending Brahmins, receiving ascetics and welcoming guests

silappathikaram:16:74-90.reading: Kannaki goes on: when his mother and his wealthy father set aside their old anger and praised her lovingly, her smile that seemed to deny the grief she hid only pained them more; though he followed unworthy ways, she, whose life does not gainsay him, rose and came; Kovalan answers by praising her, who left kin, servants and companions with modesty, innocence and chastity as her only companions and has removed his sorrow, as gold, creeper, doll of modesty and lamp of the wide earth.
silappathikaram:16:74-90.nuance: Kannaki's reply blames his conduct plainly (போற்றா வொழுக்கம் புரிந்தீர்) while setting her own rule as not opposing him (மாற்றா உள்ள வாழ்க்கை); the epic lets her name the fault and still follow. The grief she hid behind a smile before his parents is told only here. Kovalan's praise counts karpu as a companion (பெருந்துணை) in place of the kin and servants she left.
silappathikaram:16:74-90.event: Kannaki tells why she followed Kovalan, and he praises her chastity and companionship.

claims.claim: a chaste wife does not gainsay her husband even when his conduct is unworthy

silappathikaram:16:91-112.reading: Calling her the shoot of chastity, Kovalan says he will take one anklet from her small foot, go and exchange it and return, embraces her alone with burning heart and hidden tears, and leaves; walking unsteadily through the streets he does not know as an ill omen the humped bull that comes against him, since reading such signs is not his class's knowledge, and in the bazaar street he meets a goldsmith with a hundred craftsmen behind him and asks whether he can price an anklet fit for the queen.
silappathikaram:16:91-112.nuance: The narrator excuses Kovalan's blindness to the omen by his birth (தன்குலம் அறியுந் தகுதியன்று), not by his fault; the herders, whose knowledge it is, will read their own bull's tears as coming harm in the next kaathai. The goldsmith is drawn before he speaks, walking aslant (விலங்குநடை) in a tunic with tongs in hand, and Kovalan takes him for the craftsman honoured with the Pandya's name.
silappathikaram:16:91-112.event: Kovalan takes one anklet, leaves Kannaki, passes an ill omen unheeded and asks a goldsmith to price the anklet.

silappathikaram:16:113-129.reading: The goldsmith, a messenger of Death, bows and says he makes the crowns and jewels of kings, examines the anklet's workmanship, declares that it fits none but the queen, tells Kovalan to wait in his hut near the temple while he informs the king, and resolves to pass off on this stranger the queen's anklet that he himself had stolen before his theft comes to light.
silappathikaram:16:113-129.nuance: The narrator reveals the goldsmith as the real thief here, before the accusation, so the reader watches the whole frame-up knowingly. His verdict that the anklet fits only the queen is the claim the breaking of the anklet will disprove (20:74-91), since Kannaki's holds gems and the queen's pearls.
silappathikaram:16:113-129.event: The goldsmith inspects the anklet, lodges Kovalan in his hut and plans to blame him for his own theft.

silappathikaram:16:130-147.reading: The goldsmith goes on with calm hidden heart; the king, whose queen, sulking because the dances and songs of Madurai's women had captured his heart, had pleaded a headache and gone away, leaves his council for her palace with her maids, and at its gate the goldsmith falls at his feet and tells him that the thief who took the palace anklet without breaching wall or using a forked pole, putting the gatekeepers to sleep by a spell, is hiding in his hut.
silappathikaram:16:130-147.nuance: The accusation reaches the king when he has left his ministers (மந்திரச் சுற்றம் நீங்கி) to make peace with a sulking queen; the epic gives this setting without naming it a cause, and in the next lines the narrator gives the cause as the ripening of a deed. The goldsmith's tale of a thief working by mantra prepares his later lecture on thieves' arts.
silappathikaram:16:130-147.event: At the queen's gate the goldsmith tells the king that the thief of the palace anklet is in his hut.

silappathikaram:16:148-163.reading: Since it was the time for the deed to ripen, the neem-garlanded king, inquiring into nothing, calls the city guards and orders them to kill the thief if he holds the queen's anklet and bring it; the goldsmith, his purpose achieved, brings them to Kovalan, caught in the net of his ripened evil deed, and shows them the anklet, but the guards say that a man who bears himself by the marks of good birth is not one to be put to death.
silappathikaram:16:148-163.nuance: One ripening is given two subjects: the time of the deed (வினைவிளை காலம்) makes the king fail to inquire, and the net of the matured evil deed (தீவினை முதிர்வலை) holds Kovalan, so whose deed ripens is left open between them. The order கொன்றச் சிலம்பு கொணர்க condemns before any hearing. The guards' doubt is the one hesitation in the chain.
silappathikaram:16:148-163.event: The king, without inquiry, orders the thief killed; the goldsmith leads the guards to Kovalan, who they say does not look like a thief.

claims.claim: when the time for a deed to ripen comes, even a king fails to inquire
a man who bears the marks of good birth is not one to be put to death

silappathikaram:16:164-177.reading: Laughing inwardly at the guards, the goldsmith lectures them that thieves roam with eight aids, mantra, deity, drug, omen, technique, place, time and tool, and that if they use a drug the guards will suffer worse than from the king, if mantra they will be as invisible as Indra's sons, if a divine form they will show the stolen thing in hand and still go, and if they cloud the guards' eyes with drugs, the guards will not even keep their names and place.
silappathikaram:16:164-177.nuance: The real thief makes himself the expert on theft and turns the guards' good judgement of Kovalan's bearing into a sign of the thief's skill: the better the man looks, the more dangerous. The eightfold list is set out as a lore with its own order (இழுக்குடை மரபு), named a faulty tradition even in his mouth.
silappathikaram:16:164-177.event: The goldsmith lectures the guards on the eight aids of thieves.

claims.claim: thieves work by eight aids: mantra, deity, drug, omen, technique, place, time and tool

silappathikaram:16:178-193.reading: The goldsmith goes on through the other aids, that with a true omen a priceless thing falls into their hands, with technique they would take even the garland from Indra's chest, with the right place and time no one sees or stops them, with tools no one on earth can catch them, and night and day are one to them, and begins a tale of a thief who in a messenger's guise and then a woman's slipped through the dark and the lamp's shadow toward a prince's shining necklace.
silappathikaram:16:178-193.nuance: The lecture goes item by item in the order of the list (omen, technique, place, time, tool), and its claim that the thief has no refuge if one asks for his hiding place (கரவிடங் கேட்பினோர் புகலிட மில்லை) presses the guards to act at once. The unit breaks in the middle of the tale, whose verb comes in line 194.

claims.claim: a thief armed with these arts can be seen by no one, by night or by day

silappathikaram:16:194-217.reading: The goldsmith ends his tale, how the thief took the prince's necklace, dodged his sword and slipped away, and asks who in the world can match such men; a young spearman tells of a thief with a digging chisel and blue cloth who took his own sword from his hand one rainy midnight and vanished, and bids the guards do what is fit, since such men's deeds are hard to know and the king will punish them; then a drunken, unlettered guard throws his sword and cuts Kovalan across, his blood floods the ground and the earth goddess grieves, and Kovalan falls as the king's sceptre bends, his former deed come in wrath.
silappathikaram:16:194-217.nuance: The killer is not the king or the guards who doubted but a கல்லாக் களிமகன், a drunken man without learning, so the bent sceptre works through its least fit instrument. The last two lines give two causes in one sentence, the king's sceptre bent (செங்கோல் வளைஇய) and Kovalan's former deed come in wrath (பண்டை ஊழ்வினை உருத்து), the patikam's first and third morals at once. Line 210 (அலைக்கும் வேந்தனும்) is read as the king who will punish them, but the sense is not certain.
silappathikaram:16:194-217.event: After the goldsmith's and a young guard's tales of uncatchable thieves, a drunken guard cuts Kovalan down with his sword.

claims.claim: a man's former deed comes in wrath and brings his death
when an innocent man is killed at the king's order, the king's just sceptre has bent

silappathikaram:16:218-221.reading: The closing venba bids all, since both kinds of deed will surely reach them, to turn to good dharma, for the never-bending sceptre bent on earth because of Kannaki's husband, the fruit of an old deed come to ripeness.
silappathikaram:16:218-221.nuance: The moral drawn is not only that kings should judge carefully but that every hearer should do good, since good and evil deeds alike come back; the bent sceptre is made the fruit of Kovalan's old deed, which lifts the blame from the king in the same breath as it names the bending.

claims.claim: both good and evil deeds come back to their doer, so one should turn to good dharma
the bending of a just king's sceptre can be the fruit of another's former deed

links.note: Kavunthi gave Kannaki as a ward to the herdswoman and charged her to bathe, dress and mother her; Maadari here receives her as a ward, has her bathed and settles her.
links.teaches: The ascetic's charge is carried out point by point, so the refuge fails not through any lapse of the guardian but on the very day she is kept as promised, and the harm comes from the city's justice, not the host's house.

links.note: Kannaki sprinkles water on the ground as if to clear the earth-woman's distress (மண்ணக மடந்தை, line 40); at the killing the earth-woman's grief grows as Kovalan's blood pours over her (line 215).
links.teaches: The earth that Kannaki soothes with water at his last meal is soaked with his blood the same day, so the poet makes one figure measure the distance between her care and his death.

links.note: The herders liken Kovalan and Kannaki to the dark god and the lamp of their clan who relieved his distress; in the next kaathai Maadari dances the kuravai of Krishna and Pinnai so that Kannaki may see it, to ward off a coming harm.
links.teaches: The herders' wonder at their guests becomes a rite: having seen the couple as Krishna and his consort, they dance that pair's kuravai to avert the harm their omens foretell, which has already fallen.

links.note: Kovalan asks whether his ruin is illusion or a strong former deed (வல்வினை கொல்லோ); at his death the narrator answers that his former deed came in wrath (பண்டை ஊழ்வினை உருத்து).
links.teaches: The question the victim cannot answer is answered by the narrator only over his body, so the karma he half suspects is confirmed only when it can no longer be acted on, and he had meanwhile blamed himself.

links.note: The couplet says one who slipped by not guarding beforehand will grieve later over his own fault (தன்பிழை); Kovalan, now in Madurai, grieves that he grew heedless (பொச்சாப் புண்டு) and failed his parents and his wife.
links.teaches: The couplet makes late regret the heedless man's whole penalty and puts the fault in him alone, while the epic has the heedless man grieve and still lose his life, and lets him ask in the same breath whether karma rather than his own lapse has brought him here.

gains.a: Kovalan's confession gains a name and a rule: his is the heedlessness whose fruit is regret that comes too late
gains.b: the couplet gains a case where regret is not the end of the penalty, and where the one who grieves over his own fault also suspects a former deed

links.note: In Puhar Kovalan blamed his ruin on sporting with a deceitful woman and the shame of lost wealth; in Madurai he blames his own heedlessness, bad company and disobedience to his parents.
links.teaches: Between the two confessions the blame moves from Madhavi to himself, so the road to Madurai is shown changing his account of his fall even as it carries him to his death.

links.note: The couplet makes the householder the support of renouncers, the needy and the dead; Kannaki says that without her husband she lost giving to the virtuous, tending Brahmins, receiving ascetics and welcoming guests.
links.teaches: The couplet speaks of the householder as one person, while Kannaki shows that a wife alone could not keep those duties, so the householder's dharma the Kural assigns depends on the pair being together.

gains.a: Kannaki's list gains its standing: what she lost is the very support the Kural makes the householder's office
gains.b: the couplet gains its cost when the house is broken: the wife left at home cannot be the support it describes

links.note: The couplet defines the woman who guards herself, tends her husband, keeps their good name and does not flag; Kannaki hid her grief before his parents and followed him without gainsaying him though his conduct was unworthy.
links.teaches: The couplet does not say what such a wife owes a husband who wrongs her; Kannaki's answer is to name his fault and follow him all the same, so the epic shows the couplet's tireless wife carried into the ruin her husband makes.

gains.a: Kannaki's hidden grief and silence before her in-laws gain a name as keeping the household's good name, part of what defines the wife in the couplet
gains.b: the couplet gains the hard case it leaves open, a husband who has failed her, and one answer to it

links.note: In Puhar, Kannaki offered her anklets and Kovalan resolved to recover his lost wealth with them as capital in Madurai; here he takes one anklet to exchange.
links.teaches: The plan made in the bedchamber as a fresh start is carried out here and leads straight to the goldsmith, so the means of recovery chosen in Puhar becomes the instrument of his death.

links.note: Kovalan meets a humped bull in the street and does not know it as an ill omen; in the next kaathai the herdswomen see the tears of their humped bull and say a harm is coming.
links.teaches: The same beast gives the same warning to two kinds of people, and only the herders, whose knowledge it is, read it, so the epic makes reading the omen a matter of birth and has the warning understood only after the harm is done.

links.note: The goldsmith declares that the anklet fits none but the queen; in the court Kannaki's anklet, broken, shows gems where the queen's holds pearls.
links.teaches: The craftsman's expert verdict, the only evidence against Kovalan, is shown false by the anklet itself, so the case is undone by the very object it was built on.

links.note: The quatrain says that when people who know what should be known still do blameworthy things, it comes from their own former deeds; the epic says the king inquired into nothing because it was the time for a deed to ripen.
links.teaches: The quatrain traces the knowing man's wrong to his own deeds, while the epic leaves open whose deed ripens, the king's or Kovalan's caught in its net, so one man's karma may be what makes another man err.

gains.a: the king's failure gains a received explanation: knowing men do wrong when former deeds press them, and blame still attaches
gains.b: the quatrain gains a case where the deed that ripens may not be the wrongdoer's own, which its wording does not consider

links.note: The couplet calls stealth a dark knowledge (காரறிவாண்மை) absent in those who love measure; the goldsmith, the real thief, lectures the guards on the eight arts of thieves as an unmatched skill.
links.teaches: The Kural grants that stealth is a kind of knowledge, and the epic shows that knowledge turned from taking goods to taking a life, as the thief's expertise in theft persuades the guards to kill an innocent man.

gains.a: the goldsmith's lecture gains a name for what it displays: cleverness that is still darkness
gains.b: the couplet's dark knowledge gains a use it does not mention, deceiving those who keep the law

links.note: The patikam sets as the epic's third moral that a former deed comes in wrath and makes its doer eat (ஊழ்வினை உருத்துவந்து ஊட்டும்); Kovalan's death is told in the same words (பண்டை ஊழ்வினை உருத்து).
links.teaches: The moral stated as a thesis at the outset is spoken again in its own words at the death, and in the same line as the king's bent sceptre, so the epic gives its first and third morals as two causes of one event.

links.note: The quatrain says an old deed seeks out its doer as a calf finds its mother among many cows; Kovalan's former deed reaches him through a goldsmith's lie, a king's hasty word and a drunken guard's sword.
links.teaches: The quatrain's deed finds its doer by itself, while the epic shows it arriving through other people's free and blameworthy acts, so karma here does not excuse the hands it works through.

gains.a: Kovalan's death gains the quatrain's image of the deed that cannot miss its doer, which explains why every escape fails
gains.b: the quatrain's calf gains a path: the seeking deed travels through other people's lies and violence

links.note: The venba says both deeds will reach their doer and bids men turn to good dharma; Tirumular says that when the two deeds stand balanced, grace comes as the guru and frees the soul from them.
links.teaches: The venba's remedy for the two deeds is to do more good, which on its wording still returns to the doer, while Tirumular's is grace that comes when good and evil are balanced and ends them, so the pair sets merit-making against release by grace; the conflict holds if நல்லறம் is read as producing good fruit.

gains.a: the venba's moral gains a contrast that shows it offers no escape from deeds, only better ones
gains.b: Tirumular's balancing of the two deeds gains a plain statement of the view it moves beyond, that good deeds are the answer to karma

new_concepts.gloss: the vow; a religious observance or discipline undertaken
an omen or sign read as foretelling what will come
new_concepts.label_source: the unit's own word (lines 166 and 178); line 100 calls the bull's sign இழுக்கு

source_issues: Lineation: the kaathai has 221 lines as shown (217 of akaval and a four-line venba) against the edition's printed last line 215.
Lines 41, 128 and 174 carry the repair of ௌ read as ெள from old fonts (தெளித்து, வெளிப்படா, தெளிகுவர்); the repaired readings make sense.

Unit boundaries fall inside speeches: 33-47 ends in the middle of the herdswomen's question, 48-61 holds both their wonder and the start of Kovalan's speech, 62-73 and 74-90 each hold the end of one speech and the start of the reply, and 178-193 ends in the middle of the goldsmith's tale; the units are kept as cut because other chapters already link to 62-73 and 74-90.
